title: Hello, Python
objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to write and run a program that prints messages, and add comments to explain your code.

sections.title: Your first instruction: print
sections.text: A program is a list of instructions for the computer. print() is an instruction that shows something on the screen. print("Hello") shows the word Hello.

sections.title: Text goes in quotes
sections.text: Text in Python is called a string. A string must go inside quotes, like "Hello" or 'Hello'. Without the quotes, Python thinks the word is a name it should already know, and you get an error.

sections.title: Running a program
sections.text: When you press Run, Python reads your program from the top line to the bottom line, one line at a time. Each print() shows its text on a new line. If a line has a mistake, Python stops and shows an error message that tells you which line to check.

sections.title: Comments are notes for people
sections.text: A line that starts with # is a comment. Python skips comments completely. Use them to explain what your code does, or to switch a line off for a moment.

examples.title: Example 1: Say hello
examples.code:
print("Hello, Python!")
print("I am learning to code.")
examples.output:
Hello, Python!
I am learning to code.

examples.title: Example 2: Comments are skipped
examples.code:
# This program prints two lines
print("Line one")
# print("This line is switched off")
print("Line two")

diagram.title: How a program runs
steps: Python reads each line from top to bottom

options: Good morning, then Class on the next line
Good morning Class on one line
check_questions.explanation: Each print() shows its text on a new line, so you see Good morning and then Class below it.

misconception.1: Every print() starts a new line.
misconception.2: print shows the text inside the quotes, not the code itself.
misconception.3: print() shows text on the screen, so something is printed.

check_questions.prompt: Which line correctly prints the word Hello?
check_questions.explanation: Text needs quotes, print is written in small letters, and the text goes inside round brackets.

misconception.0: Without quotes, Python thinks Hello is a name and shows an error.
misconception.1: Python cares about capital letters. Print is not the same as print.
misconception.3: In Python 3, print needs round brackets around what you want to show.

check_questions.explanation: The lines that start with # are comments, so Python skips them. Only print("B") runs.

misconception.0: Lines that start with # are skipped.
misconception.2: The first and last lines are comments, so they do not run.
misconception.3: The middle line is not a comment, so it runs.

try_it.title: Try It Yourself
try_it.instructions: Change the message so it says hello to your class. Then add a second print() line that shows your favourite food, and a comment that explains your program.
